### What It Achieved and Where It Failed

The Non-Aligned Movement's greatest achievement was **legitimizing the idea that newly independent nations had the right to determine their own path** — neither client states of Washington nor satellites of Moscow.

In practice, this legitimacy was contested at every turn. The CIA overthrew Mossadegh (Iran, 1953), Arbenz (Guatemala, 1954), and Lumumba (Congo, 1960). The Soviet Union crushed Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968). Both superpowers demonstrated that non-alignment was tolerated only when it didn't threaten their core interests.

The movement still exists, with 120 member states. It has never recovered the moral clarity of Bandung.

sources.label: Vijay Prashad, The Darker Nations (2007)
Roeslan Abdulgani, The Bandung Connection (1981)
Christopher Lee, Making a World After Empire (2010)

title: Patrice Lumumba: Murdered by the Cold War
tldr: Patrice Lumumba became the first Prime Minister of an independent Congo on June 30, 1960. He was dead by January 17, 1961 — assassinated with the direct involvement of the CIA, Belgian intelligence, and Congolese political rivals. He had been in office for 77 days. His murder set the template for Cold War interference in African politics and condemned the Congo to 32 years of Mobutu's kleptocracy. He is the symbol of what African independence could have been.
body:
## Seventy-Seven Days

Patrice Émery Lumumba was 34 years old when he became the first Prime Minister of the Republic of the Congo on June 30, 1960 — the day Belgium granted independence to its Central African colony after 75 years of some of the most brutal colonial rule in history.

His independence day speech, delivered in the presence of Belgian King Baudouin who had just given a speech praising Leopold II's "civilizing mission," was not diplomatic:

> *"We have known the back-breaking work exacted from us in exchange for salaries which did not allow us to eat enough to drive away hunger... We have known the mockeries, the insults, the blows that we had to undergo morning, noon, and evening because we were Negroes."*

The speech shocked the Belgian delegation and electrified Africans across the continent. It also marked Lumumba as a target.

### The Congo's Strategic Value

The Congo was not simply a large African country. It was one of the most resource-rich territories on earth:
- **Uranium** from the Shinkolobwe mine — the same uranium used in the bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
- **Cobalt, copper, diamonds, gold, rubber**
- Control of the Congo River basin — the agricultural and hydrological heart of Central Africa

Lumumba's stated intention to use Congolese resources for Congolese development — and his willingness to ask for Soviet assistance when Belgium and the United States withheld support — made him, in CIA Director Allen Dulles's words, "a Castro or worse."

### The Assassination

Within weeks of independence, the Congo was in crisis: Belgian troops re-entered the country, the mineral-rich Katanga province seceded with Belgian support, and the Congolese army mutinied. Lumumba turned to the United Nations for help; the UN secretary-general, Dag Hammarskjöld, refused to act against the Belgian intervention.

Lumumba then requested direct Soviet assistance. This was the pretext the United States needed.

In August 1960, CIA Director Dulles sent a cable to the CIA station in Leopoldville: Lumumba's "removal" should be "an urgent and prime objective." A CIA operative carried **poison** to Leopoldville with orders to introduce it into Lumumba's food or toothpaste.

The poison was never used — Lumumba was deposed in a CIA-backed military coup by Colonel Mobutu Sese Seko in September 1960 before it could be deployed. He was captured, tortured, and on January 17, 1961 — shot and his body dissolved in acid.

Mobutu ruled the Congo (which he renamed Zaire) for 32 years, one of Africa's most corrupt and brutal dictatorships, consistently supported by the United States throughout the Cold War.

sources.label: Ludo De Witte, The Assassination of Lumumba (2001)
Georges Nzongola-Ntalaja, The Congo from Leopold to Kabila (2002)
David Van Reybrouck, Congo: The Epic History of a People (2014)

title: Frantz Fanon: The Psychiatrist Who Theorized Revolution
tldr: Frantz Fanon was a Martiniquais psychiatrist working in colonial Algeria who became the 20th century's most important theorist of anti-colonial revolution. His two major works — Black Skin, White Masks and The Wretched of the Earth — argued that colonialism was not just political and economic domination but psychological mutilation, and that genuine liberation required both the end of colonial structures and the psychological reconstruction of colonized people. Every liberation movement of the 1960s–1970s read him.
body:
## The Doctor Who Diagnosed Colonialism

Frantz Fanon arrived in Algeria in 1953 as a psychiatric resident at the Blida-Joinville Hospital. His job was to treat the mentally ill. What he found was that the colonial system itself was the pathology.

### Black Skin, White Masks (1952)

Fanon's first major work, written while he was still a student in France, is a psychoanalytic examination of what colonialism does to the mind of the colonized.

His central argument: **the colonized person is not simply dominated — they are alienated from themselves.** Colonial education, language, and culture teach the colonized person that their own history, beauty, and ways of knowing are inferior. The colonized person internalizes this judgment. They begin to experience themselves through the colonizer's eyes.

Fanon called this "lactification" in the Caribbean context — the aspiration toward whiteness as the standard of value — and argued it was a form of psychological violence more damaging than physical coercion, because it made the colonized complicit in their own subjugation.

The cure, Fanon argued, was not assimilation — the French model, which offered colonial subjects the possibility of becoming French — but **the recovery of a pre-colonial identity and the construction of a new national consciousness**.

### The Algerian War and Political Radicalization

In 1954, the Algerian War of Independence began. As the war intensified, Fanon found himself treating both French torturers and their Algerian victims — sometimes in the same week. He resigned from his hospital position in 1956, writing a letter to the Algerian Governor-General that is one of the great documents of colonial resistance:

> *"If psychiatry is the medical technique that aims to enable man no longer to be a stranger to his environment, I owe it to myself to affirm that the Arab, permanently an alien in his own country, lives in a state of absolute depersonalization."*

He joined the FLN (Algerian National Liberation Front) and became its representative to sub-Saharan Africa.

### The Wretched of the Earth (1961)

Fanon's final work, written while he was dying of leukemia and published weeks before his death, is addressed directly to the colonized of the world. It contains three arguments that defined a generation of revolutionary thought:

1. **Decolonization must be violent** — not because violence is desirable, but because colonial structures cannot be negotiated away; they must be dismantled by force, and the experience of revolutionary violence is itself psychologically transformative for the colonized
2. **The national bourgeoisie is the enemy** — newly independent nations that replace white colonizers with a Black or brown elite that maintains the same extractive economic structures have not been decolonized
3. **A new humanism is possible** — but only if liberation movements reject both European values and pre-colonial romanticism and build genuinely new social forms

Fanon died on December 6, 1961. He was 36.

sources.label: Frantz Fanon, The Wretched of the Earth (1961)
Frantz Fanon, Black Skin, White Masks (1952)
David Macey, Frantz Fanon: A Biography (2000)

title: Pan-Africanism: The Idea That Built a Continent's Politics
tldr: Pan-Africanism — the idea that all people of African descent share a common identity and destiny and should work toward collective liberation and unity — was not born in Africa. It was born in the Caribbean and the United States, in the minds of diaspora intellectuals who experienced anti-Black racism and concluded that it was a global system requiring a global response. From W.E.B. Du Bois to Kwame Nkrumah to the African Union, the 20th century's African politics cannot be understood without it.
body:
## The Idea Born in Exile

Pan-Africanism, one of the 20th century's most consequential political philosophies, was not developed on the African continent. It was developed in **Trinidad, Jamaica, the United States, and London** — by people of African descent who had been removed from Africa by the slave trade and who experienced, in the diaspora, the global nature of anti-Black racism.

The insight was simple and devastating: the oppression of Black people in Alabama, Jamaica, Senegal, and South Africa was not a local problem with local causes. It was a **single global system** — the system that the Doctrine of Discovery had codified, the slave trade had built, and colonialism was maintaining. A local response to a global system would fail. Only a global response would work.

### The Founding Figures

**Henry Sylvester Williams** (Trinidad) organized the first Pan-African Conference in London in 1900 — the first international gathering of people of African descent to discuss their shared condition.

**W.E.B. Du Bois** (United States) became the movement's most important intellectual force for the next five decades. His concept of "double consciousness" — the sense of "always looking at oneself through the eyes of others" — described the psychological condition of diaspora Africans with precision that resonated globally. He organized five Pan-African Congresses between 1919 and 1945.

**Marcus Garvey** (Jamaica) took Pan-Africanism to the masses. Where Du Bois organized intellectuals, Garvey organized workers. His Universal Negro Improvement Association had **6 million members** at its peak — the largest Black organization in history. His Back to Africa movement was dismissed by the Black establishment but electrified the diaspora.

### From Philosophy to Politics

The 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester, organized by Du Bois and attended by a young **Kwame Nkrumah** (Ghana) and **Jomo Kenyatta** (Kenya), was the pivot point where Pan-Africanism transformed from diaspora philosophy into African political program.

Nkrumah, who became Ghana's first president in 1957, made Pan-African unity the explicit goal of his foreign policy. He hosted the **All-African Peoples' Conference** in 1958 — the first gathering of African nationalist movements from across the continent — and argued that political independence without continental economic unity was meaningless.

His vision found partial institutional expression in the **Organization of African Unity (OAU)**, founded in 1963, and its successor, the **African Union (AU)**, founded in 2002. Neither has achieved the continental integration Nkrumah envisioned — but both exist because he argued for them.

sources.label: W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903)
Imanuel Geiss, The Pan-African Movement (1974)
Colin Legum, Pan-Africanism: A Short Political Guide (1962)

title: Structural Adjustment: The Policy That Broke Developing Nations
tldr: In the 1980s, the IMF and World Bank began conditioning debt relief on a standardized package of economic reforms: cut government spending, privatize state enterprises, deregulate markets, liberalize trade. Applied to 70+ countries across Africa, Latin America, and Asia, these Structural Adjustment Programs dismantled public health systems, eliminated agricultural subsidies, and transferred national assets to foreign buyers — all in the name of economic efficiency. A generation of development was lost.
body:
## The Debt Trap

The story of Structural Adjustment begins with the 1973 oil crisis. Petrodollars — the sudden windfall to Arab oil states — flowed into Western banks, which lent them aggressively to developing nations at low interest rates. In the late 1970s, US Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker raised interest rates dramatically to combat American inflation. Developing country debt, much of it in dollars at floating rates, became instantly unpayable.

The result was the **debt crisis of 1982**, triggered by Mexico's announcement that it could not service its foreign debt. Country after country followed. The IMF and World Bank were the lenders of last resort.

### The Washington Consensus

The conditions attached to IMF and World Bank loans became known as the **Washington Consensus** — a term coined by economist John Williamson in 1989 for the standard policy package that the Washington-based institutions required:

1. **Fiscal discipline**: Cut government deficits by reducing public spending
2. **Tax reform**: Broaden the tax base and reduce marginal rates
3. **Financial liberalization**: Eliminate interest rate controls
4. **Trade liberalization**: Remove tariffs and import quotas
5. **Privatization**: Sell state enterprises to private buyers
6. **Deregulation**: Remove regulations that restrict market competition
7. **Property rights**: Strengthen legal protection of private property

The logic was coherent in theory: efficient markets would allocate resources better than state enterprises; open trade would create comparative advantage; fiscal discipline would eliminate inflationary pressure.

### What Actually Happened

The application of these policies to the specific conditions of African and Latin American economies produced results that the models had not predicted:

**Healthcare:** Cuts to government health spending and user fees for previously free services reduced access for the poor. Studies found **increased infant mortality** in multiple countries during SAP implementation.

**Agriculture:** Elimination of agricultural subsidies and state marketing boards — which had stabilized prices for smallholder farmers — exposed them directly to world commodity price volatility. Import liberalization flooded local markets with subsidized American and European agricultural products that local farmers could not compete with.

**Industry:** Tariff removal dismantled nascent manufacturing sectors before they could become competitive. The import-substitution industrialization strategies that had driven East Asian development were explicitly prohibited under SAP conditionality.

**Asset transfer:** Privatization, conducted rapidly without functioning financial markets or regulatory capacity, often resulted in state assets being sold below value to foreign buyers or domestic political elites.

### The Reckoning

By the late 1990s, even the IMF's own internal evaluation office was producing reports acknowledging that SAPs had failed to produce sustained growth in most recipient countries and had worsened inequality and social indicators.

The policy consensus shifted — toward the "Post-Washington Consensus" that emphasized institutions, governance, and "pro-poor growth." The damage, however, was already done: a decade and a half of dismantled public infrastructure, eliminated development capacity, and transferred assets that have not been returned.

sources.label: Joseph Stiglitz, Globalization and Its Discontents (2002)
Fantu Cheru, African Renaissance (2002)
Dambisa Moyo, Dead Aid (2009)

title: Das Kapital: The Book That Tried to Explain Everything
tldr: Karl Marx spent 40 years in the British Museum trying to understand why industrial capitalism produced poverty alongside unprecedented wealth. Das Kapital, published in 1867, was his answer: capitalism is not a natural order but a historical system built on the exploitation of labor, prone to cycles of crisis, and destined to be replaced. Half the world was governed in its name by the 20th century. No idea in modern history has been more consequential — or more contested.
body:
## The System That Needed Explaining

By the 1840s, Britain's Industrial Revolution had created the most productive economy in human history — and also some of the most miserable living conditions ever recorded. Manchester cotton workers labored 14-hour days in toxic factories. Children worked in coal mines. Life expectancy in industrial cities was lower than in pre-industrial ones.

The dominant economic theory — classical liberalism — said this was temporary and self-correcting. The market would eventually equilibrate. Wages would rise. Conditions would improve.

Karl Marx thought this was wrong, and he spent the rest of his life explaining why.

### The Core Argument

Marx's analysis begins with a deceptively simple question: where does profit come from?

In a market economy, goods exchange at their value. If I trade a coat for boots, I presumably get equivalent value. How, then, does a capitalist end up with more value than he started with? If he buys materials and labor at their market price and sells the finished product at its market price, where does the surplus come from?

Marx's answer was **surplus value**: the capitalist pays workers for their labor power (the ability to work), not their labor (the actual work performed). A worker paid enough to survive for a day can produce, in that day, far more value than their subsistence costs. The difference — the surplus — is appropriated by the capitalist as profit.

This was not theft in the legal sense. It operated through the wage contract, willingly entered into. But it was, Marx argued, exploitation in a structural sense: the entire edifice of capitalist profit rested on the systematic extraction of unpaid labor from the working class.

### The Contradictions

Marx argued that capitalism contained internal contradictions that would produce recurring crises:

**The tendency of the rate of profit to fall**: as capitalists competed with each other by replacing labor with machinery, the source of surplus value (labor) diminished relative to total investment — driving profit rates down over time and producing periodic crises of overproduction.

**The immiseration of the proletariat**: as capital concentrated in fewer hands, workers were progressively impoverished — not necessarily in absolute terms, but relative to the wealth being generated.

**The centralization of capital**: competition would drive weaker capitalists out of business, concentrating ownership in larger and larger corporations — creating the conditions for collective ownership.

### What Happened Next

Marx died in 1883 having seen none of this confirmed by events. Within 35 years of his death, a revolution in his name had seized Russia. By 1980, states claiming Marxist ideology governed roughly one-third of the world's population.

What those states actually built — and whether it bore any resemblance to what Marx had theorized — remains the most contested question in modern intellectual history.

What is less contested: Das Kapital changed what questions economists were required to answer. The 20th century's welfare states, labor regulations, and social insurance programs were built in part by people trying to prove Marx wrong by making capitalism more humane.

sources.label: Karl Marx, Das Kapital Vol. 1 (1867)
Francis Wheen, Karl Marx: A Life (1999)
David Harvey, A Companion to Marx's Capital (2010)
